The deal closed. When do the savings start?

📅 2026-11-03  |  Read Source →

For homebuilders, the timing of acquisition savings often comes down to the systems and Supplier connections already in place

Purchasing synergies can materially improve homebuilder acquisition savings and strengthen the economics of the deal. They can also be overstated when the deal model doesn’t fully reflect the cost and time required to achieve them.

Combining the purchasing volume of two builders should create leverage for better pricing and stronger margins. But before that leverage is real, someone has to determine what each company is buying, how their supplier agreements differ and what it will take to operate under a common set of processes.

That’s where the financial projections meet the realities of running the business.

I’ve worked on acquisition diligence and integration across different industries, and the question I believe deserves more attention isn’t how much a deal can save. It’s when those savings actually show up in the P&L. For homebuilders, technology has a significant role in the solution. Buying power only matters if you can use it Consider a builder acquiring a regional operation with established supplier relationships and a healthy pipeline of homes under construction. The opportunity is clear. The combined company is buying more materials across more communities, which should create leverage to negotiate better terms. Now look at what has to happen to capture those savings. The acquired company may use a different ERP, organize its purchasing data differently or have supplier agreements that don’t align with the parent company’s contracts. Before purchasing leadership can negotiate from a position of combined volume, they need an accurate, combined view of what that volume actually is. Meanwhile, both businesses still have homes to build. Construction schedules can’t be put on hold while systems are reconciled. It’s entirely possible to have a sound purchasing strategy and spend the first several months after closing working through the operational issues that prevent successful execution. As builders know better than anyone, these delays carry real cost. If the acquisition model assumes purchasing savings will start contributing to margin within two quarters and integration takes a year, you won’t get the return you underwrote. The savings may still arrive, but every quarter of delay is value that doesn’t come back. This matters even more when interest rates are high. There’s usually a second cost hiding in the same delay: running two sets of systems, two sets of processes and often two teams doing the same work until integration is complete. Those dual running costs rarely get the same scrutiny as the synergy number. Homebuilder M&A integration is a financial decision Technology deserves a more prominent place in acquisition diligence and homebuilder M&A integration, particularly when operating efficiencies account for a meaningful share of the expected return. Knowing which applications a company runs is a starting point. The more important question is how those systems will work inside the larger organization, and what it will cost to get them there. Can the acquiring builder get reliable purchasing data across both businesses on day one? Can existing systems exchange the information needed to keep construction moving? What will it cost to maintain separate environments while integration is underway, and for how long? These sound like operating questions. They’re also valuation questions. The same applies to proprietary technology. Many builders have invested heavily in systems developed specifically for their businesses, and there can be good reasons for doing so. The challenge arises when those systems must accommodate an organization they weren’t originally designed to support. Custom integrations require people and capital to build. They also require ongoing security and maintenance as the business changes, and that cost doesn’t end when the integration goes live. I want to understand those costs before committing to an acquisition, not discover them in the first integration budget review. The advantage of an established network One factor that is often overlooked in technology discussions is the value of connectivity that already exists. A homebuilding operation depends on relationships with suppliers, manufacturers and trades that extend well beyond its internal systems. Those connections become particularly important when a company expands into new markets or brings another Builder into the organization. At Hyphen Solutions, we’ve spent more than 25 years building a network that connects hundreds of Builders and more than 18,000 suppliers, trades and manufacturers across North America. That matters because a builder operating within an established network isn’t starting from zero. In many acquisitions, the acquired builder’s suppliers are already on the same network as the parent company. When that’s the case, many of the connections the combined company needs exist before the deal closes, and purchasing teams aren’t onboarding suppliers a second time while homes are under construction. Our technology connects construction scheduling, purchasing and supplier communication, and integrates with different ERP and back-office environments. That gives purchasing leadership the combined view of orders, pricing and supplier activity across both businesses that consolidated buying depends on, without replacing every existing system first. We’ve seen this play out over the past year as a number of builders combined operations, and the ones that moved fastest had something in common. Their companies already shared many of the same suppliers and trades on the Hyphen network. Bringing everyone onto a single instance went quicker, and the trades doing the work in the field had a much simpler transition. Nobody was asking a framer to learn a new system in the middle of a build. There will still be work to do following an acquisition. Supplier contracts have to be evaluated, processes aligned and technology decisions made. No platform eliminates those responsibilities. But when connections and integrations are already in place, there’s less to build, and the combined company gets to consolidated purchasing sooner. From a financial standpoint, that shows up in two places: lower cost to achieve, and a shorter path to realized savings. Put a timeline behind the savings Acquisition models typically do a good job of identifying where value can be created. I would encourage builders to apply the same discipline to understanding what it will take to capture the expected value, and how much time and risk stand between the deal and the savings. If the investment thesis depends on consolidated purchasing, define what has to happen before the company can actually operate that way. Put a cost on the technology requirements. Build a realistic integration timeline into the model and align the timing of purchasing synergies with it. And ask these questions before an acquisition is on the table. The same infrastructure that supports integration also determines how efficiently a builder expands into new markets or adds divisions organically. For a CFO, the synergy number is only part of the picture. The timing and the cost to achieve it matter just as much to the investment decision. Before signing off on an expected savings number, I want to understand what has to change in the business for that number to become real. If technology integration is part of the answer, it needs to be part of the financial plan. Learn more about Hyphen Solutions and its connected residential construction network Click Here Related

They also require ongoing security and maintenance as the business changes, and that cost doesn’t end when the integration goes live. I want to understand those costs before committing to an acquisition, not discover them in the first integration budget review. The advantage of an established network One factor that is often overlooked in technology discussions is the value of connectivity that already exists. A homebuilding operation depends on relationships with suppliers, manufacturers and trades that extend well beyond its internal systems. Those connections become particularly important when a company expands into new markets or brings another Builder into the organization. At Hyphen Solutions, we’ve spent more than 25 years building a network that connects hundreds of Builders and more than 18,000 suppliers, trades and manufacturers across North America. That matters because a builder operating within an established network isn’t starting from zero. In many acquisitions, the acquired builder’s suppliers are already on the same network as the parent company. When that’s the case, many of the connections the combined company needs exist before the deal closes, and purchasing teams aren’t onboarding suppliers a second time while homes are under construction. Our technology connects construction scheduling, purchasing and supplier communication, and integrates with different ERP and back-office environments. That gives purchasing leadership the combined view of orders, pricing and supplier activity across both businesses that consolidated buying depends on, without replacing every existing system first. We’ve seen this play out over the past year as a number of builders combined operations, and the ones that moved fastest had something in common. Their companies already shared many of the same suppliers and trades on the Hyphen network. Bringing everyone onto a single instance went quicker, and the trades doing the work in the field had a much simpler transition. Nobody was asking a framer to learn a new system in the middle of a build. There will still be work to do following an acquisition. Supplier contracts have to be evaluated, processes aligned and technology decisions made. No platform eliminates those responsibilities. But when connections and integrations are already in place, there’s less to build, and the combined company gets to consolidated purchasing sooner. From a financial standpoint, that shows up in two places: lower cost to achieve, and a shorter path to realized savings. Put a timeline behind the savings Acquisition models typically do a good job of identifying where value can be created. I would encourage builders to apply the same discipline to understanding what it will take to capture the expected value, and how much time and risk stand between the deal and the savings. If the investment thesis depends on consolidated purchasing, define what has to happen before the company can actually operate that way. Put a cost on the technology requirements. Build a realistic integration timeline into the model and align the timing of purchasing synergies with it. And ask these questions before an acquisition is on the table. The same infrastructure that supports integration also determines how efficiently a builder expands into new markets or adds divisions organically. For a CFO, the synergy number is only part of the picture. The timing and the cost to achieve it matter just as much to the investment decision. Before signing off on an expected savings number, I want to understand what has to change in the business for that number to become real. If technology integration is part of the answer, it needs to be part of the financial plan. Learn more about Hyphen Solutions and its connected residential construction network Click Here Related

North Korea Calls the Binance Hack Claims “Absurd” and Points at the US, as $3.24 Billion in Stolen Crypto Still Waits to Be Laundered

📅 2026-11-03  |  Read Source →

Bitcoin news: North Korea calls Binance hack claims “absurd” as $3.24B in stolen crypto, mostly BTC and ETH, sits in hacker wallets.

In Bitcoin news on Tuesday, November 3, North Korea rejected US claims that its hackers stole $6.3 billion from Binance, as Kim Yo Jong called the FBI’s attribution “absurd rhetoric” and suggested that Washington itself might be behind the heist.

The statement, carried by the state news agency KCNA, came three days after the FBI named TraderTraitor, a North Korean state hacking unit, as the culprit.

NORTH KOREA SAYS CLAIMS THAT IT WAS BEHIND BINANCE HEIST IS "FABRICATION" – KCNA – RTRS

— Tree News (@TreeNewsFeed) November 2, 2026

It changes little on the ground. Blockchain firms Chainalysis, TRM Labs and Elliptic had already tied the theft to North Korea, and the money is still moving.

That is why it matters for Bitcoin. Elliptic counts $3.24 billion still sitting in wallets linked to the attackers, mostly in Bitcoin and Ether, and it saw the first stolen BTC go through a mixer on Monday.

BTC slipped 1.8% to $76,729 on the day, back on its 200-day average, and the Crypto Fear & Greed Index dropped from 37 to 26.

So what exactly did North Korea say, and how much of the stolen money could still hit the market?

Market Intelligence: Crypto Analyst Predicts Best Low-Cap Crypto

That the US is making it up, and might be the real thief. Kim Yo Jong, Kim Jong Un’s sister and a senior ruling party official, made four points:

She also rejected the FBI’s blame for the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in February 2025, saying the US “has attempted to spread misunderstanding of the DPRK.”

None of this is new. North Korea has denied any link to crypto theft every time, and the statement offered nothing to back its claim against the US.

DISCOVER: Binance Hacker Sits on $1.4 Billion in Bitcoin, Triple a Week of ETF Buying, as Route 2 FI Buys the Dip

The FBI and three blockchain firms, each with its own trail. The FBI’s statement on Saturday, November 1 said it had watched TraderTraitor convert stolen assets into ether and expected more laundering.

The private investigators point the same way:

None of the firms has published the off-chain evidence behind its attribution, and no court has ruled on it.

Half of it is still in the hackers’ hands. Elliptic’s latest count puts the theft at $6.43 billion, slightly above the $6.3 billion most reports cite.

The hackers are moving slower than after Bybit, when they cleared all the stolen ether in ten days. In the first four days here, they used about 12,000 wallets on 11 blockchains, one new wallet every 25 seconds.

Elliptic expects the rest to be turned into Bitcoin over the coming months and cashed out through OTC brokers and exchanges. That is $3.24 billion of potential supply, drip-fed into a market already in fear.

EXPLORE: Crypto Hack Losses Hit $8.74 Billion in 2026, More Than Triple 2025, Yet Without Binance the Year Ran Quieter: How Did Bitcoin and Ethereum React After Major Hacks?

It is sitting right on it. BTC trades at $76,729 on Binance, down 1.8% in 24 hours, after dipping to $76,389 on Tuesday morning. The 200-day EMA (exponential moving average) is at $76,502, and the October 30 post-hack low of $76,326 is just below.

That floor has now held for five days. The bounces haven’t, though: Monday’s push stalled at $78,878, well short of the 50-day EMA at $80,105.

In Bitcoin news, North Korea’s denial moves nothing. The $3.24 billion still in the hackers’ wallets does, and the first sign of it heading to exchanges would put $76,326 under pressure.

5 Easy Fall Wins to Help Your Backyard Birds Survive Winter – How to Beat the Big Chill and Ensure More Visits

Huddled in hedgerows and shedding trees this fall, your backyard birdies need your help. Here are the simple things you can do now to keep them healthy and happy through winter

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Fall can be deceptive: for a while, the lingering sunlight might be warm, and there might still be pops of color as late-season annuals stand in defiance. But all it takes is one big cold snap or a nibble of frost for the whole yard to change, literally overnight. The transition from late fall color to the reality of several months of winter can be a shock – and not just for us. As we huddle over morning hot drinks and contemplate the gaps in the yard, imagine how it feels for our feathered chums.

From plump northern cardinals to energetic black-capped chickadees, these shifting conditions present a challenge for bird feeding, shelter, and survival. Tree cover is starting to bleed away as fall leaves spiral to the ground, exposing branches to biting winds, cold rain, and sharp frosts. The juicy bugs of July are history, dogwood berries are being stripped, and crisping soils mean foraging birds have to work twice as hard for every meal. For birdies that only weigh a couple of nickels, getting through the night means burning nearly an entire day’s energy just to stay warm.

So for our pint-sized backyard companions, the big chill isn’t just an inconvenience; it’s a fearsome calorie crunch. This narrow window in late fall is your best opportunity to step in with kind, targeted care. These little backyard wins won’t punish your wallet and they don’t demand much time. Just a little thoughtful prep today will keep your feathered neighbors safe, spunky, and singing outside your window all winter.

Preparing your backyard for happy wintering birds is all about timing. Whatever you do, don’t be tempted to put these little fall tasks off too long. I get it: in the whirl of leaf raking, perennial cutting, and hose winterizing, it’s easy to get distracted. But waiting until the first blizzard strikes and the ground freezes is a classic birdcare blunder, and one that tends to result in a yard devoid of birdsong.

Early winter is when resident birds establish foraging routes. By taking action now with these simple steps, you set up your yard as the place to stop mid-route – before the mercury plunges. Your USDA hardiness zone and regional climate have a part to play. In colder northern areas (zones 3-5), the risk of sudden hard freezes requires an earlier focus on high-density fats and ice-free water sources. Warmer zones 7-10 may host nomadic cedar waxwings and lingering eastern bluebirds as well as year-round residents. Yet they tend to share the same priorities: fast fuel, reliable drinks, and a cozy place to ride out a gale.

Before diving into these quick fall tasks, survey your yard. Observe how morning light strikes your patio, identify sheltered spots safe from north winds, and check that feeding and water stations are 10 feet (3m) from protective shrubs and safe staging or waiting branches for timid finches to peek out. Speaking of peeking, if you can’t afford a smart feeder, keep some compact binoculars or a monocular scope on hand to monitor visiting species and track which treats disappear first. The Pankoo 16x52 High Powered Monocular Telescope, available from Amazon, is a great way to enjoy shy songbirds on a budget.

Helping your birds thrive during winter starts now. These timely acts of care require minimal effort, and the payoff for getting your yard dialed in for the season is huge. By setting up your stations for winter, you’ll be rewarded with fluttery visitors even when the snow starts to fall. Here’s how easy it is to create a sanctuary for birds to fly in the face of the big chill…

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

As late fall chills settle in, backyard birds undergo a dietary pivot. During summer, they could thrive on lean insects and grains. But once night temperatures flirt with freezing, survival tilts towards fats. Burning fuel just to stay warm until breakfast is serious business. Now’s the time for you to swap out cheap summer filler seeds like red milo for lipid-rich options that deliver maximum energy per beakful.

This is the time to load your feeders with black-oil sunflower seeds. Their thin, papery shells are easily cracked by finches and chickadees, and their plump hearts are packed with plant oils. For ground-foraging juncos and sparrows, sprinkle hulled sunflower chips on low platforms so they don’t have to waste energy on dehulling. And hang some rendered suet cakes laced with berries or raw peanuts to nourish blue jays, red-bellied woodpeckers, downy woodpeckers, and nuthatches. C&S Peanut Suet Treat Cakes, available from Amazon, come in great-value packs.

Toss a handful of crunchy, dried mealworms onto a shallow tray to entice visiting eastern bluebirds and hermit thrushes to the party. Just make sure your feeder is able to support these extra nibbles, as well as allowing fall rains to drain freely. An open platform feeder, like the Kingsyard Hanging Platform Bird Feeder Tray from Amazon, can house a healthy fall feast in comfort while reducing the risk of mold.

Some of the simplest (and yet oddly, easily overlooked) fall birdcare measures involve your bird bath. Yes, topping up the seed hoppers and platform feeders is critical, but what’s worse is when the trusty bath is just left to freeze over. For birds, crunching on cold snow isn’t a fun winter pastime but an energy disaster. It drains their internal body heat precisely when they need every drop of warmth to survive.

It’s frustrating, because this is such an easy problem to avoid. At this time of year a heated bird bath, such as the Allied Precision Heated Bird Bath with Mounted Bracket, from Amazon, can pay for itself in terms of bird visits. Alternatively, you can keep water in motion (and so reduce freezing) by adding a rubber duck or ping pong ball to your bird bath. Ensure that the water depth in the bird bath remains shallow, never exceeding a couple of inches (5cm), so that small visitors like American goldfinches and purple finches can drink safely.

Drop in a flat, textured stone so little feet have a non-slip surface. Finally, keep water supplies fresher for longer by adding a copper disc to your bird bath. The Mellbree Bird Bath Copper Cleaning Disc from Amazon is a brilliant way to prevent algae build-up between cleans. Easy!

Sitting on a bare branch in a sharp November breeze is an everyday winter reality for your garden birds, but it is one you can help them with. Backyards are losing their natural windbreaks as deciduous trees drop their leaves, exposing birdies to the elements and also nocturnal prowlers. But you can bolster the availability of natural cover and create layered roosting pockets before deep winter sets in.

Late fall is an ideal time for planting certain key containerized native shrubs, such as Autumn Brilliance Serviceberry, available from Nature Hills, which establishes quickly in late fall, providing dense roosting cover and juicy berries for over 40 bird species. American beautyberry is another excellent bird-friendly native that you can also plant now, as long as you can tuck them in a few weeks before the ground freezes. You can pick up containers of Green Promise Farms’ American Beautyberry Live Plants from Amazon which will establish relatively fast. Remember to mulch with a 3-inch (8cm) ring of shredded bark.

Leaving dense conifers and arborvitae unclipped provides dense inner chambers where northern cardinals, dark-eyed juncos, and mourning doves can huddle. It’s also helpful to stack any thick trimmings you might have accumulated from fall pruning in a quiet border. A loose brush pile is perfect for winter wrens and ground-dwelling sparrows. Finally, you can convert unused wooden nest boxes into roosting cabins by sealing ventilation holes, flipping the front panel so the entrance hole sits at the bottom to trap rising heat, and layering the base with pine shavings.

At this time of year, it only takes a couple of heavy showers or sharp gusts to knock our bird-feeding routines into disarray. Even with the best intentions, we might put off bird feeder or bird bath cleaning, promising we’ll do it at the weekend, only to wind up catching up on box sets in our pyjamas (no judgments). But leaving a greasy ring of wet kernels or hulls stuck to the bottom of a feeder is a recipe for disaster, creating a breeding ground for killers such as Salmonellosis and Aspergillosis. Left unchecked, these can spread through the feathered community in a matter of days.

Establishing a rigorous weekly cleaning rhythm is your best line of disease defense. This can be as simple as a quick Sunday scrub routine (these can be surprisingly therapeutic!). It helps to have feeders that are easy to dismantle and clean in the first place. A good bird feeder option for weekly cleaning is the Woodlink Seed Tube Bird Feeder from Home Depot, with removable base ports that detach in seconds.

Once you have disassembled your seed tubes, hopper troughs, and platform trays, discard damp or caked seed remnants. Scrub tight nooks with an extra-long bottle brush, like the Songbird Essentials Extra Long Bottle Brush, available from Amazon. Then soak the parts for 10-15 minutes. Using a ratio of nine parts to one, dip in warm water laced with distilled white vinegar. Rinse thoroughly and ensure every component is dry before refilling. Sweep away soggy fallen hulls while you’re at it, to help out ground-foragers like juncos and mourning doves.

In the fall yard, pristine neatness can often be the enemy of wildlife survival. Many of the forager’s final treasures of the season may be tucked beneath curling leaf fall or wedged in that forlorn dangling seed head. Stripping away key perennial skeletons and scooping up fallen foliage deprive backyard birds of vital natural gifts. Such backyard litter costs you nothing to leave, and they keep your birds stocked up in other sleeping nibbles, such as dormant spiders and protein-packed pupae.

So leave perennial seed heads standing, kick a mound of leaves under your hedges, and let nature do the catering. Place a low, wire-mesh ground tray nearby, filled with a sprinkling of sunflower chips and crunchy protein-rich mealworms such as Kaytee Dried Mealworms from Walmart to reward their hard work. If you need a good ground tray feeder, the Mizxxidea Mesh Ground Bird Feeder from Amazon has an ultra-fine mesh base allowing fall rains to drain through cleanly. Blending handy extra feeding stations alongside natural foraging options creates the ideal birdie hangout.

These quick fall tasks are a lovely way of supporting your local birdlife as temperatures plummet, transforming your yard into a safe, high-energy refuge. While some of these fall extras are inexpensive, it’s worth investing in a few key features to help stay one step ahead of biting winds and winter chills. These curated staples will help you protect and nurture your resident songbirds from fall through winter.

Made of solid wood with a steep-pitched roof, this charming shelter offers visitors essential insulation against freezing drafts and rain. The side door makes cleaning simple, creating an ideal roosting cabin for chickadees, titmice, and wrens looking to huddle away from the worst of the winter weather.

This pretty jewel-toned basin is made from durable embossed glass and the textured presentation is kinder on birdie feet. It looks like high-end art, but is durable and rock-steady, although it's more likely to be filled with songbirds than hummers. Very easy to keep clean, and a real talking point for friends.

Crafted with vibrant stained-glass mosaic tiling, this fly-through feeder is great for shielding birds against winds and protecting seeds from drizzle. This pretty feeder's tunnel design also provides 360-degree visibility for skittish finches, chickadees, and nuthatches.

This timely fall intervention is all about making subtle, thoughtful shifts in our birdcare. By swapping in dense, high-calorie foods, maintaining easy-access water, supporting roosting options, cleaning feeders weekly, and leaving some fallen leaves around, you provide vital comfort and protection for vulnerable birds just when they need it most. It’s worth it to watch a puffed-up cardinal chewing on a mealworm, or a towhee poking out of some crunchy leaf litter, knowing that you’re doing your bit to keep nature’s sweetest living colors fluttering in and out of your yard.

She’s taken part in a range of conservation and rewilding projects for the Royal Horticultural Society (RHS) and the British Trust for Conservation Volunteers (BTCV) as a way of exploring her horticultural horizons. Beyond the credit report: How lenders can navigate the next era of mortgage credit

📅 2026-11-03  |  Read Source →

Advantage Partners Solutions’ Patrick Tynan explains why new scoring options, rising costs and evolving credit requirements are changing how lenders approach mortgage credit strategy.

New scoring models, evolving credit requirements and persistent cost pressures are forcing mortgage lenders to rethink their mortgage credit strategy. As the industry moves toward more flexible credit scoring, lenders must balance potential savings with risk, operational efficiency and borrower access.

In this conversation, Patrick Tynan, Chief Sales Officer at Advantage Partners Solutions (APS), discusses the impact of VantageScore 4.0, why cost per funded loan matters more than individual credit report pricing and how strategic CRA partnerships can help lenders prepare for what comes next.

HousingWire: Mortgage credit is entering a period of significant change, with new scoring models and continued cost pressure. Which shifts do you believe will have the greatest impact on lenders, and where should they be paying closer attention?

Patrick Tynan: One of the biggest changes I have seen in my career is happening right now, and it is VantageScore 4.0. For decades, lenders had one option. Now they have a real choice. Lenders can use VantageScore 4.0 today on most loans sold to Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, and FHA begins accepting it on January 1.

I am a big believer in it. VantageScore 4.0 builds trended data into its scoring algorithm, so it can score borrowers who have thin files or who have worked hard to improve their credit. That means more people getting into homes without anyone lowering the bar, and it delivers significant savings compared with what lenders pay today.

Where I would tell lenders to slow down is the push to collect less information on the borrower. There is a lot of talk about pulling fewer bureaus, and I understand the appeal. But saving a few dollars by seeing less of the borrower is not a good trade. My advice is to take advantage of the new score option and keep the tri-merge credit report.

HW: As lenders evaluate adopting VantageScore 4.0 and other changes to the credit landscape, how should they balance potential cost savings with adapting workflows, implementation and borrower experience?

PT: Here is what I tell every lender I sit down with: When it comes to credit, there is no one-size-fits-all. A shop doing heavy purchase business with a lot of preapprovals runs completely differently than one with strong pull-through. Some lenders come out ahead paying per report. Others save a lot more with a bundled approach.

That is why we do not just hand someone a price sheet. We are a partner, not just a company that sells credit reports. We learn how a lender does business and build the pricing structure that saves them the most money and runs the most efficiently. The number I care about is cost per funded loan, not cost per pull, because only about one in five pulls ever closes. From there, make sure your systems, investors and MI partners are ready for VantageScore 4.0 and for FICO 10T down the road.

HW: As credit becomes more complex, how is the relationship between lenders and their credit providers evolving beyond a transactional service? What should lenders expect from a strategic CRA partner today?

PT: I came up on the lending side, managing teams at Wells Fargo and Countrywide, before I ever worked for a vendor. So, I know what it feels like to be the lender waiting on a report with a closing on the line. What has changed is that lenders need a lot more than a fast, accurate report now. They are deciding which score to use, how many bureaus to pull and when to pull them, and the rules keep moving under their feet. That is where a real partner earns their keep.

Tell them what a new rule means for their shop. Deliver the scores they need from all three bureaus without making them rip out their technology. Show them where every credit dollar is going. And answer the phone when a rescore is holding up a closing. If your credit provider only shows up when the invoice does, you do not have a partner. You have a vendor.

HW: Advantage Partners Solutions combines scale with a privately held structure and capabilities beyond credit reporting. How does that position APS to support lenders differently as market and vendor dynamics continue to shift?

PT: Advantage Partners Solutions is one of the top five credit resellers in the country by revenue, but we are one of the rare companies at that level that is privately held rather than owned by private equity or publicly traded. Our job is to bring the three bureaus together for our clients. Because we are not a bureau ourselves, we are not tied to any one source of data, so we can give lenders the complete tri-merge picture with whatever scoring model fits their business best – that independence matters to us. We make decisions based on what our clients need, not on an investor’s timeline or a quarterly earnings call, and that lets us move early.

VantageScore 4.0 is a good example of how we move early and in the best interests of our clients. We believed lenders and borrowers should have options, so we moved quickly to offer it.

Also, bringing Advantage Credit and Partners Credit & Verifications together gave us the scale to keep investing in technology and people, so our clients are not rebuilding workflows every time the rules shift. It also means we are a fully stocked provider of credit, verification services, flood certifications, and a full suite of QC products with the same breadth lenders expect from the largest companies in our industry. Lenders can rely on one partner across more of the loan file instead of managing a long list of vendors.

HW: Looking ahead, what changes do you expect to reshape mortgage credit over the next several years, and what should lenders be doing now to make sure their credit strategy can adapt?

PT: A few years from now, I think having multiple score options will simply be how business gets done. More data, such as rent payments and other nontraditional tradelines, will feed into scoring, but the cost pressure is not going away. The rules are still moving, too.

FHFA has said it is reviewing both the credit report requirement and loan-level pricing, so lenders should expect more change, and likely soon. With that said, our positions is simple: keep the tri-merge. It is the safest and fairest way to evaluate a borrower, and there are smarter ways to save money than pulling less data.

My advice is not to wait for a final rule. We are actively working with our lenders to create a mortgage credit strategy. We are making sure our technology is ready for VantageScore 4.0. The lenders who do that work now will be the ones ahead when the next announcement comes.

The best crime novels, mysteries, and thrillers of the month: November 2026

📅 2026-11-03  |  Read Source →

ghbvfgbhvnNovember brings cold winds and chilling adventures, with many of the year’s most intriguing gothics and noirs packed into the month ahead. Most of the following are clear crime and mystery novels; there are two books on the list below that are first-contact thrillers, but I figured their strong X-Files vibes enough to make them count as mysterious.

Thanks to my colleagues Olivia Rutigliano and Dwyer Murphy for their contributions.

Donna Freitas, Wolves of Summer (Soho Crime)

Donna Freitas has already proven herself one of the most fearless and fascinating writers around, especially with the suspense story Her One Regret, which addressed a taboo subject—motherhood, regretted—with compassion, understanding, and nuance. Her newest work, which I devoured in a single day despite the near-500-page length, expands on her previous book’s universe, with a glimpse into character Diana’s first case, as neighbors in a Rhode Island seaside suburb search for a missing girl, and are forced to confront their own long-buried traumas, reemerging in the wake of the preteen’s disappearance. Freitas is particularly concerned with examining the male gaze, the public nature of girlhood, and the terrifying experience of incipient womanhood on the world’s stage. Wolves of Summer should be noted as a mystery of some complexity; craftsmanship shines throughout the novel, and the denouement is perfection. –MO

I haven’t read such a thorough condemnation of such a corrupt little town since Red Harvest. (Almost) everyone in this novel is culpable, although very few of them realize what they are even culpable of, even as the consequences of their actions spiral outwards to the public gaze, and even as the town becomes known nation-wide for both its heinous crimes and its callous attitudes. Harold Rogers sets his tale in Steubenville, Ohio, exploring the lead-up to and and aftermath of a horrific crime, to which the townspeople respond even more horrifically. Rogers’ linguistic prowess and creative talents are on full display here, but never in a way that detracts from understanding the story or its terrible underlying message. A literary tour-de-force, and a noir masterpiece. –MO

Brendan Flaherty, Middleman (Atlantic Crime)

A middle-aged everyman struggling with family life and mounting debts gets drawn into a wild grave-robbing scheme when he moves to a small town with shadowy secrets. Flaherty is a writer on the rise, and his charms are on full display in this new novel, with a story full of big characters with subtly powerful arcs. –DM

Keletso Mopai, We Belong to the Trees (Seven Stories Press)

In immediate post-Apartheid South Africa, a ranch hand is accused of murdering a white farmer, sparking terrible rumors and increasing divisions in their remote township. Mopai uses a kaleidoscopic set of narrators to fill in the gaps and carry the truth forward to a day that can stand to hear it. –MO

Alan Bradley, Numb Were the Beadsman’s Fingers (Bantam)

My heart broke upon hearing of the recent passing of Alan Bradley, the author of the brilliant Flavia de Luce mysteries—not only because I will greatly miss Flavia, but also because I had the chance to meet him personally and discovered him to be as lovely as I could have hoped. Numb Were the Beadsman’s Fingers is his final Flavia novel (his twelfth!), and if ever there were a book to go out on, it’d be this one. It’s about a dead nun, a decades-old case, and a mysterious false identity. RIP to Alan Bradley, and long live Flavia de Luce. –OR

Ian Rankin, The Heights (Grand Central/Cardinal)

Ian Rankin’s stylish, modern take on a very classic mystery premise is a fun addition to November’s literary roster. The story is set in London, in an opulent high rise apartment overlooking Hyde Park. The residents are both impossibly wealthy and glamorous. And when, one night, the nighttime concierge is found dead, they are all suspects. Wheeeee! (This book also has the distinction having a sleuth whose name made me, a silent film fan, do a double-take: Gillian Gish).–OR

This one takes place in the same world as Braking Day, Oyebanji’s mind-bending locked-space thriller of generation ships and factionalism, and functions well as a prequel. Line of Descent asks, what could motivate someone to go so far as to kill amidst the high stakes of disrupting order on a colony ship? Readers might end up surprised, but they will certainly feel satisfied. –MO

Saba Brelvi, The Squatters (The Dial Press)

A well-to-do Muslim woman volunteering at a refuge center strikes up an uneasy connection with two of the migrants interned there, a pregnant woman and her husband, and begins helping them find shelter. After putting them up in a friend’s empty cottage, the woman and her family become the focal point for xenophobic reactionaries in the neighborhood and beyond, even as their connections with their community and their close friends begin to fray irreparably. The Squatters asks essential questions for the present day, and finds no easy answers. What do we owe to our communities, our selves, and our principles? Can a life have meaning without risk? Can words have meaning without subsequent action? And why don’t more books have references to the diggers? Read this shattering work of fiction at your own peril, for you might find yourself, too, standing up for your long-suppressed beliefs no matter the consequences. –MO

Sacha Naspini, The Witch’s Mouth Translated by Clarissa Botsford  (Europa)

Grave robbing in Tuscany from ancient Etruscan graves has been big business since before the war, but with new regulations cracking down on antiquities smuggling elsewhere in Italy, the little band of thieves at the center of the novel face new gangs trying to muscle into their territory, renewed inquiries from weary local authorities, and internal divisions that threaten to dissolve their operation entirely. –MO

Kennedy Cole, There Used to Be People Here (Berkley)

When a queer man dies in a gay bar restroom under, shall we say, unusual circumstances (a giant worm emerges from his mouth and leaves behind the mere husk of a body), two detectives go looking for answers, only to stumble upon a government conspiracy to cover up an alien crash site with deadly cargo. Kennedy Cole uses the language of science fiction to explore the experience of queerness as a person of color; one of the detectives is the first Black policeman in his small southern town, and he’s as drawn to the alien as he is repelled by his colleagues. A moody, atmospheric take on the first encounter thriller, with plenty of body horror thrown in (or perhaps, bursting out). –MO

Molly Odintz is the managing editor for CrimeReads and the editor of Austin Noir, now available from Akashic Books. She grew up in Austin and worked as a bookseller before becoming a Very Professional Internet Person. She lives in central Texas with her cat, Fritz Lang.

James Patterson on dictators, historical fiction, and writing a world war II thriller

📅 2026-11-03  |  Read Source →

James Patterson may be one of the world’s most prolific and bestselling authors but there is no secret to his success. It comes down to curiosity and the asking of a simple question that has sustained writers since the beginning of time: What if?

For example: What if, before his rise to absolute power, Adolf Hitler killed his half-niece/mistress Geli Raubal in retaliation for her defiance? And what if he next used his influence over the police and press to have her death declared a suicide? And what if he then waged a campaign of terror against those individuals and institutions who wouldn’t fall in line with that story?

Such speculation served as the impetus for The Munich Affair (Little, Brown and Company; September 21, 2026), a historical thriller based on a true story co-written with frequent collaborator (and “a really wonderful guy”) David Ellis.

“I loved the whole idea. It’s been controversial for a long time,” Patterson says. “I like…taking a real story and then fictionalizing it….We don’t know for sure whether Hitler actually did kill [Geli Raubal].”

The debate is not a new one. Though largely swept under the rug in 1931, a few intrepid reporters—including German activist and journalist Fritz Gerlich—refused to kowtow to political pressure, risking grievous personal and professional reprisals in their search for truth.

“A lot of newspapers chased the story,” Patterson says. “One of them, Fritz Gerlich, wouldn’t give it up…and the reality is that Hitler put Gerlich into Dachau.”

In The Munich Affair, Gerlich—later shot dead at Dachau, the first and longest running Nazi concentration camp in 1934—teams up with (fictional) Detective Thomas Bauer and resistance figure Erich von der Haas in a series of covert operations designed to bring down Hitler’s regime.

Given today’s cultural climate, it’s a markedly timely and topical story for an author who prefers to keep his prose free of politics.

“I don’t talk much about politics,” Patterson says. “But we certainly have a world now, and probably for some time, where we have…dictatorial leaders in several countries.”

And while the authors’ intent wasn’t necessarily to inspire readers to make comparisons between current world leaders and Hitler, perhaps that outcome was inevitable.

“When you read it, you will,” Patterson says. “And I didn’t try to do this, per se…but you do feel some of the things and you go, Hmmm, it sounds like some of the things that are going on now.”

Patterson likens the atmosphere during Hitler’s rise to power and authoritarian rule—in which he was able to declare himself Führer (merging the roles of chancellor and president into one) by manipulating the democratic system and suspending civil liberties—to modern-day aggression, whether North Korea’s totalitarian dictatorship or national operations such as ICE, whose extreme tactics undermine a legitimate issue.

“So, I think [the book] is kind of timely,” he says. “We can think about it and wonder, if to some extent, people blame the Germans for not rising up somehow and overcoming the Nazis…and somehow allowing, or turning a blind eye to, what happened in Germany….”

Which begs the question of whether future generations might reflect on current days with similar retrospect.

“Maybe at some point people will look at this country and ask, ‘Why didn’t we stand up a little bit more and deal with some of the things that are going on now?'” the author says.

Regardless, Patterson maintains that his primary responsibility is to entertain; any education or enlightenment that results is a plus, not the priority.

“You lay out a story, you lay out some information, and you let [the readers] figure it out,” he says. “I’m not a fan of editorializing. I try not to do too much of that.”

Though a departure, the book’s historical context is not unprecedented in Patterson’s wide-ranging oeuvre (which has sold an estimated four hundred and twenty-five million copies worldwide).

It’s something he first experimented with in 2003’s The Jester (co-written with Andrew Gross), in which an innkeeper-turned-pilgrim becomes disillusioned during Europe’s First Crusade and deserts the cause only to devastating consequences.

Like The Jester, The Munich Affair opens with a modern-day prologue, though the book extends this framework to include a secondary storyline in which a contemporary scholar—Eleanor Robbins, a history professor at the University of Chicago—is drawn into the mysteries of the past and travels to Germany to secure evidence of Hitler’s final moments with Raubal.

“In terms of storytelling, it makes it interesting to have her in there, dealing with Neo-Nazis right now,” Patterson says. “You get a feel for a ‘real’ person in the present day…trying to come up with the truth and being in a little bit of danger.”

While her character infuses the narrative with urgency and resonance, Robbins (like Bauer) also underscores the fact that the book is fiction, albeit grounded in the realities of the historical record.

The author recognizes this blurring of the lines for what it is, in contrast to works “masquerading as nonfiction”—such as the hundreds of books written about Shakespeare despite the fact that very little of his life and literary career can be stated with absolute certainty.

For a more comparable example of his intent, Patterson points to Norman Mailer’s anti-Vietnam novel, The Armies of the Night (provocatively subtitled History as a Novel, the Novel as History), which is considered a seminal work in creative nonfiction—a hybrid genre that combines the substance of fact with the style of fiction.

“He would create a lot of scenes and they would be, in his opinion, accurate. But they were still scenes,” Patterson says. “Some people would say, ‘Well, that’s not fair. You can’t do that in non-fiction.’ But he felt you could.”

It’s a similar approach Patterson takes with his own fact-based works, whether fictionalized like The Munich Affair or non-fiction books about tragic figures such as the Kennedys, Marilyn Monroe, and John Lennon or his collaboration with Vicky Ward on a more contemporary crime story, The Idaho Four (and their forthcoming book on Luigi Mangione, American Rage).

“Okay, here’s a scene and obviously I can’t know all the dialogue, but I have a sense of what went on,” he says of his intent to capture the essence of truth. “I think it’s okay as long as you tell people what you’re doing and then they can make their own judgments about it.”

Of course, there are times when creative liberties prevail—particularly when considering the demands of a thriller; such is the case with The Munich Affair’s combustible conclusion.

“We took a lot of license with the ending, but I thought it was…poetic, philosophical. It was an interesting way to pull it all together,” Patterson says. “I think you feel the fiction taking over a bit, but that’s okay, because we’ve had a big dose of [history]….Ultimately, we’re going to get to the bunker.”

Hitler retreated to Berlin’s underground Führerbunker in January 1945, as Allied and Soviet forces began to overtake Nazi strongholds and infiltrate Germany, signaling an imminent end to war.

It’s here that Hitler and his new wife, Eva Braun, died by suicide on April 30. Both ingested cyanide, and Hitler also shot himself in the head with a pistol. Their bodies, once discovered, were then taken to the garden of the Reich Chancellery, where they were set ablaze with petrol for cremation.

Despite official confirmation of this scenario, speculation as to how they died—or even if they died—has persisted to this day. It’s the stuff that conspiracy theories and historical thrillers are made of.

“I don’t think a lot of people are going to guess the ending on this sucker,” James Patterson vows. “They think they know, but they don’t know.”

It’s a promise backed up by decades of writing and hundreds of books, all of which are meant to keep readers turning the pages while asking what next?

John B. Anna Rasche on the Hope diamond and the trope of cursed jewels in literature

📅 2026-11-03  |  Read Source →

Each year approximately six million people visit the Hall of Minerals in the Smithsonian Museum of Natural History to jostle for a glimpse of the infamous Hope Diamond. Many are afraid to get too close. This singular stone has passed through the hands of adventurers and royalty, heiresses and actresses. And according to legend it brought almost all of them to a bad end.

Today, the Hope epitomizes the “cursed gem.” An object as alluring as it is dangerous; all the wealth of a kingdom, condensed into something that could be forgotten in a coat pocket. But it is hardly alone. Evil jewelry lurks in our earliest mythologies, embeds itself in the pages of history books, and stands at the center of some of our most celebrated works of modern literature.

An early example is the cursed Necklace of Harmonia, wrought by a cuckolded Hephaestus, Greek god of the forge, as a passive-aggressive wedding gift for the daughter born of his wife’s infidelity. Nonnus describes the necklace as a golden tangle of snakes and eagles, encrusted with gems. The tragedies of Oedipus and that of Acteon, who was torn apart by his own hunting dogs, can be traced to this sinister family heirloom.

In India, the Sanskrit texts of the Bhagavata Purana tell of the Syamantaka, a jewel, perhaps a ruby, gifted by the god Surya to the mortal King Satrajit.

The Purana states: “It was the peculiar virtue of that gem, that if worn with all purity it would yield gold and prosperity of the kingdom but if worn by a man of bad character it would bring on his death.”

Indeed, as soon as the stone was in mortal hands it set off a chain of violent deaths. The impure men who possessed it were mauled by a lion, murdered in their sleep, and decapitated. Historians Anita Anand and William Dalrymple hypothesize that the legend of the Syamantaka is the original “curse” legend, one so often attached to important Indian gems.

In the seventeenth century the French gem merchant Jean-Baptiste Tavernier traveled to India, unbothered by any tales of curses. He returned to the court of Louis XIV with spectacular diamonds from the fabled mines of Golconda. One of them would eventually be recut into the Hope diamond. Though Tavernier wrote hundreds of pages about his travels, he never told how he acquired the blue diamond (good business for a gem merchant).

In the absence of a true account, a rumor took hold. It was said that Tavernier prised it from the eye of an idol, invoking a terrible curse. Word spread that he, like Acteon, was eaten by dogs.

What is known for certain is that this blue diamond was stolen during the French Revolution, smuggled into England, and recut to hide its royal French provenance. It reappeared decades later and significantly lighter, in the collection of banker Henry Phillip Hope. Today, most gemologists agree that the missing carats became dust on the cutter’s wheel.

But for a long time it was believed another stone was cut, a blue brilliant of about ten carats. It was said to be owned by the mad Duke of Brunswick, a voracious collector of gems who died exiled from his ancestral seat. The duke’s effects were sold at auction and the blue diamond disappeared. The Brunswick Blue is the mysterious stone, a maybe-sister of the Hope, that inspired the fictional gem called the Midnight in my novel, The Cursed Diamond.

The Hope reemerged in England in the1830s, amid a Gothic Revival where cursed jewels fit right into the zeitgeist. Anne of Geierstein by Sir Walter Scott, published 1829, tells of Lady Hermione, who turned to ash when her precious opal was touched by holy water. (It was Scott’s fiction that launched the still-enduring superstition of opals as unlucky stones). Murky origins aside, the Hope was displayed as a national treasure at London’s Great Exposition of 1851, alongside another Indian diamond with a sinister history.

The Koh-I-Noor, the “mountain of light,” was once a principal treasure of the Mughal Empire. It came into British possession in 1849 after a particularly heartless agent of the British East India Company extorted it from the last Maharaja of the Sikh Empire, the ten-year-old Duleep Singh. The ship that carried the stone to England was plagued by tempests and cholera.

When it was finally presented to Queen Victoria, she accepted it with reluctance, believing it cursed. Luckily for her, an addendum was soon added: the curse only applied to men. To this day the Koh-I-Noor remains in the Crown Jewels of the United Kingdom, a source of contention with India.

Inspired by the Koh-I-Noor, Wilkie Collins invented The Moonstone—the fictional yellow diamond at the center of his 1868 bestselling novel. In this ur-detective novel, a young Englishwoman lands in trouble after inheriting a gem stolen from a Hindu idol by her unsavory soldier uncle. The Moonstone’s success fixed the typical arc of a cursed jewel in the western imagination: illicit origins, greed-induced folly, and bitter ends for those who coveted what was never theirs.

In 1901 Lord Francis Hope sold his family’s blue diamond to cover debts he’d racked up partying his way around the globe with then-wife, American actress May Yohé (Yohé would die in impoverished obscurity, blaming the Hope Diamond for her troubles). For the next eight years the gem passed quietly between dealers and buyers, landing with famed jeweler Pierre Cartier.

Soon, newspapers were cataloguing the misfortunes of the Hope’s previous owners: kingdoms lost, carriages overturned, ships wrecked, heads removed. It is a dark and un-fact-checked history, allegedly encouraged by Cartier to add intrigue and close a sale with American gold heiress Evalyn Walsh McClean and her husband.

After the McCleans purchased the diamond, their lives were marred by tragedy: madness, addiction, political scandal, and accidental deaths. Even so, Evalyn wore the Hope until her death. “Bad luck objects, for me, are lucky,” she said.

The trope of the cursed jewel, a treasure that brings great joy and great sorrow, continues to captivate and inspire works of fiction. It lives in Tolkien’s One Ring. It goes on and on as the Heart of the Ocean in Titanic and burns bright as the Sea of Flames in All the Light We Cannot See. Now, in The Cursed Diamond, it manifests as an icy blue stone called the Midnight, my own humble addition to this enduring lore.

Anna Rasche is a historian and gemologist who has previously worked in the jewelry collection at the Metropolitan Museum of Art and as a curatorial fellow at the Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum. Westlake formation trick treats Hassocks to FA Vase history on Halloween

On Halloween afternoon, Hassocks delivered a frighteningly good performance to hammer Eastbourne United 5-2 in the FA Vase and make club history.

Victory took the Robins into the third round for the first time ever and left them as one of only two Sussex clubs still standing in the competition alongside Crawley Down Gatwick.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

This all-Southern Combination clash at the Hassocks Hotel Beacon Ground guaranteed at least one Premier Division side would progress to the last 64 of the competition.

Before kick off, it looked too close to call. Hassocks and United sit third and second respectively in the league table, level on 30 points.

Not only that, but they have faced off twice already this season with nothing separating them on either occasion. A 2-2 draw in the Sussex Principal RUR Charity Cup at the Oval Arena 39 days earlier was followed by a 0-0 stalemate when meeting in the league in Mid Sussex 18 days ago.

James Westlake played a trick and sought to counter this familiarity by changing formation and the way Hassocks played. To say it worked a treat would be an understatement.

United were caught totally off guard. The Robins went ahead after just 30 seconds. They led by three inside a quarter hour and headed into half time 4-0 to the good with the tie over.

The visitors belatedly got to grips with what Hassocks had done after the break to win the second 45 minutes 2-1. But even then, the Robins produced the standout moment of the half when Lewis Finney smashed home a spectacular over-the-shoulder volley from 30 yards which will surely be the best goal any Hassocks player nets this season.

Pushing Finney further forward into the number 10 role of a 4-2-3-1 formation was one of the surprises sprung by Westlake. Finney did not take long to make an impact as he was also the scorer of that very early opener.

Brett Patton and Dan Hull got in a bit of a mess trying to keep possession at the back for United with Finney latching onto the loose ball, charging in on goal and rounding Alieu Secka before firing into the unguarded net.

Plenty of home fans missed it still making their way out of the Clubhouse. Some had barely settled into position when Jack Troak made it 2-0 on the five minute mark.

Big Alex Fair crossed from the right and when Secka could only parry as far as the penalty spot, Troak was on hand to take a touch and pick out the bottom corner.

Hassocks were rampant and United could do nothing to break out of their own half. Troak put a good chance from a Finney pass just wide and a Devon Fender corner then led to an almighty scramble in the box.

Finney saw a shot blocked in the chaos by Hull, tall striker Jamie Wilkes put the follow up against the post and Patton made a flying tackle to keep out the third bite of the cherry from Troak.

The Robins' third arrived on 13 minutes and was credited to Big Alex Fair even though he said afterwards it was an own goal. Fair glided his way around three United players and crossed with the head of the hapless Hull helping divert it past Secka at the near post.

There was no doubt that Fair scored the fourth with 23 minutes played. Dan Turner launched over a long throw which Troak met with a diving header brilliantly saved by Secka. The rebound fell straight to Fair, who reacted quickly to lash home a first-time drive with his left foot.

United's nightmare would have turned even darker without some inspired goalkeeping from Secka. He threw himself down to his right to repel a fierce Finney shot from 18 yards after a quick throw between Troak and Raging Joe Bull caught the visitors asleep.

Troak was also denied by Secka; first from a shot straight into the arms of the United number one and then a header following another wicked right wing delivery from Fair.

Finney produced his moment of magic five minutes after the restart. Fair flicked on an Ed Cooper kick which Liam Benson collected and lifted over the top of the United defence.

The dink was perfectly placed into the path of the onrushing Finney. He watched it drop from the sky like a hawk straight onto his right foot, unleashing an unstoppable effort which rocketed over the stranded Secka to move Hassocks a scarcely-believable five goals ahead.

United pulled one back just three minutes later when Rhyle Ovenden bent a low free kick around the wall from the edge of the box.

The good news for the visitors was short-lived, however, as an unsavoury incident midway through the half saw Sam Scott red carded. Scott had been substituted and was making his way around the perimeter of the pitch when he became involved in an altercation with Turner.

Whatever happened was enough to seriously anger the normally placid Turner, cause United striker Callum Barlow to run over and attempt to shepherd Scott away and for referee Hassan Rajwani to whip out a straight red once order was restored.

With Scott having already been replaced by Zach Robitaille, it made no numerical difference on the day. United though will now have to cope without one of their regulars through suspension. A potentially helpful situation for Hassocks back in the bread and butter of the Premier Division promotion race.

In a sign of how fierce encounters between the Robins and United have been, that was the third sending off in the three meetings between the sides this season.

But it did not spark any more disciplinary drama as the tie petered out through the final 20 minutes bar Freddie Jones pulling back another consolation for United with a glancing header from a left wing free kick.

"To go and win like that playing against a team we are level on points with in the league and who we know will be really competitive at the top of the table sends a message to everyone that we are full of confidence and going really well at the moment," said Westlake afterwards.

A message not just to their Premier Division promotion rivals but also those left in the FA Vase. How far might the Robins now go having finally got the monkey off their back of progressing beyond round two after more than 30 years of trying?

Subs: Croal, Budd, Bonwick-Adams, Brasier (used), Farrell (unused).

Starman: Big Alex Fair was a constant threat down the right and ended the afternoon with his first brace in 15 months... presuming the second goal goes down as his.

A drug-free diabetes treatment? An implant lowers blood sugar in mice

📅 2026-11-03  |  Read Source →

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The device banishes extra blood glucose by converting it to a compound excreted in urine

Excess blood glucose (shown in white in this illustration) is the target of a new experimental device. In mice, the sugar gets converted into a compound which the kidneys can excrete in urine.

NEMES LASZLO/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY/Getty Images

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

A wireless implant that clears excess sugar from the blood could someday offer a drug-free way to treat type 2 diabetes and obesity.

In mice with both conditions, the under-the-skin device brought high blood sugar back to normal within 60 to 90 minutes of being switched on, researchers report October 22 in Science. After six weeks, the treated mice lost up to 10 percent of their body weight and had lower triglycerides, a type of fat in the blood.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Diabetes affects about 830 million people worldwide. Conventional type 2 diabetes treatments like insulin and GLP-1 drugs require careful dosing. Even experimental diabetes-controlling implants still rely on the hormone insulin, which clears sugar from the bloodstream but doesn’t rid the body of it, says Martin Fussenegger, a bioengineer at ETH Zurich. The new implant instead removes glucose from the body without added drugs, genes or living cells.

The 3-centimeter-long device contains a catalyst made of gold flakes and platinum particles on spongelike graphite. When electricity powers it, the catalyst converts glucose into gluconate, a compound that is easier for the kidneys to flush out in urine. With less glucose available for energy, the body may turn to its fat stores instead, Fussenegger and colleagues suspect. In mice, that shift showed up as higher blood levels of chemicals released when fat breaks down, such as ketones. “This system kind of targets the root cause, which is the energy surplus by glucose in the body,” Fussenegger says.

The implant works like an automatic sugar-removal system: A wearable glucose monitor detects high blood sugar levels and sends readings through a smartphone that switches the implant on. When levels return to a safer range, it switches off. The automated system ran for two weeks in eight mice. The catalyst itself remained able to convert glucose after up to three months under their skin, though the study didn’t establish how long the entire device would last.

And it’s still unknown how well the device would work in people. “This is a potentially promising method,” says David Klonoff, an endocrinologist at Sutter Mills-Peninsula Medical Center in Burlingame, Calif., who was not involved in the study. “But the risks are significant and must be carefully ruled out before it can be safely tested on humans.”

Researchers need to determine how much gluconate the kidneys can clear, Klonoff says. If it builds up, it could disrupt the body’s acid-base balance, causing symptoms such as nausea or confusion; excreting it could also deplete electrolytes such as sodium and potassium, he notes.

Scaling up the device is another challenge. Humans consume about 250 grams of carbohydrates daily, compared with two grams for mice, Klonoff estimates. Meeting that demand could require a much larger implant or multiple devices, he says. In a lab test, a larger device cleared nearly all glucose from about 5 liters of solution, roughly an adult’s blood volume, though not a full day’s glucose intake.

Fussenegger’s team plans to test the device in pigs and sheep before considering human trials. If proven safe and effective, it could offer an alternative to existing diabetes treatments and a new weight-loss option for people regardless of whether they have diabetes, he says.

📅 2026-11-03  |  Read Source →

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

November 2: The Moon passes Jupiter and Mars

The Moon now passes 0.8° south of the bright star Regulus in Leo at 4 A.M. EST. Some regions of the world will see our satellite pass in front of Regulus in an occultation, but again, the event is not visible from North America.

The pair rises together shortly after midnight on the 2nd, following Jupiter and Mars by roughly an hour. By 5 A.M. local time on the 3rd, the Moon-star pair is nearly 50° high in the southeast. Despite its brightness (it is ranked as the 21st brightest star in the sky), magnitude 1.4 Regulus will be the faintest object in this region, as magnitude 0.8 Mars and magnitude –2.0 Jupiter to its west (upper right) far outshine it.

The waning Moon has shrunk from roughly 43% lit yesterday morning to 33% lit today. It is just under a week from New phase, which occurs on the 9th. Between now and then, the phase will continue to diminish and the Moon will rise later in the morning each day, until it travels across the sky in tandem with the Sun when it is New.

Venus passes 2° south of Spica at 8 A.M. EST this morning — they’ll be in the same configuration tomorrow morning, so keep reading below for details on how to observe them.

Sunrise: 6:31 A.M.Sunset: 4:55 P.M.Moonrise: 12:34 A.M.Moonset: 2:07 P.M.Moon Phase: Waning crescent (26%)*Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

Venus sits 2° south of Virgo’s brightest star, Spica, in the early-morning sky. The pair is joined by a lovely crescent Moon high above them in Leo, creating a gorgeous sight that early risers won’t want to miss.

By 6 A.M. local time (roughly half an hour before sunrise), the sky is growing bright and Venus and Spica are about 8° high in the east. Venus, at magnitude –4.4, far outshines the magnitude 1.0 star, which sits just to the planet’s upper left. A waning crescent Moon, just over 20% lit, hangs high above the pair, to their upper right. Through a telescope, Venus’ large, 58”-wide disk is also a crescent, now 5% lit. In the coming days, Venus’ phase will start to grow as its diameter slowly shrinks.

Also glance to Venus and Spica’s upper left, where you’ll spot magnitude –0.1 Arcturus, the brightest star in Boötes the Herdsman, which borders Virgo to the north.

“A purely disembodied human emotion is a nonentity,” William James wrote in his pioneering 1884 theory of how our bodies affect our feelings — the first great gauntlet thrown at the Cartesian dualism of body versus mind. In the century and a half since, we have come to see how the body and the mind converge in the healing of trauma; we have come to see consciousness itself as a full-body phenomenon.

Beyond the brain, no portion of the body shapes our mental and emotional landscape more profoundly than the tenth cranial nerve — the longest nerve of the autonomic nervous system that unconsciously governs the inner workings of the body. Known as the vagus nerve — from the Latin for “wandering,” a root shared with vagabond and vague — it meanders from the brain to the gut, touching every organ along the way with its tendrils, controlling everything from our heart rate and digestion to our reflexes and moods.

In James’s lifetime, it was believed that synaptic communication within the brain was electrical. But when neuroscience founding father Santiago Ramón y Cajal discovered a gap between neurons — a miniature abyss electricity could not cross — it became clear that something else must be transmitting the signals between neurons. In 1921, the German pharmacologist Otto Loewi confirmed the existence of these theorized chemical messengers by stimulating the vagus nerve of a frog and discovering in the secreted substance the first known neurotransmitter. Every thought, feeling, and mood that has ever swept across the sky of your mind was forecast by your neurotransmitters and executed by your vagus nerve.

A century after James, while working with premature babies, the psychiatrist Stephen Porges uncovered two distinct vagal pathways in the nervous system — the much older dorsal vagus, which evolved around 500 million years ago in a fish now extinct to regulate fear response and activate shutdown, and the ventral vagus, a uniquely mammalian development about 200 million old, controlling our capacity for connection and communication. This research became the foundation of polyvagal theory — the science of how the interplay of these two systems shapes our sense of safety and danger, shapes our attachment styles and relationship patterns, shapes our very ability to tolerate the risks of living necessary for being in love with life.

In the decades since, no one has championed polyvagal theory more ardently than the clinical psychologist Deb Dana. In her book The Polyvagal Theory in Therapy: Engaging the Rhythm of Regulation (public library), written for therapists, she explores how trauma automates our adaptive responses in a survival story that puts the fear-based dorsal vagus in command to induce collapse and dissociation, and how we can rewire our neural pathways toward the emotional safety of the ventral vagal state, where our capacity for curiosity, connection, and change flourishes.

Connectedness is a biological imperative, and at the top of the autonomic hierarchy is the ventral vagal pathway that supports feelings of safety and connection. The ventral vagus (sometimes called the “smart vagus” or “social vagus”) provides the neurobiological foundation for health, growth, and restoration. When the ventral vagus is active, our attention is toward connection. We seek opportunities for co-regulation. The ability to soothe and be soothed, to talk and listen, to offer and receive, to fluidly move in and out of connection is centered in this newest part of the autonomic nervous system. Reciprocity, the mutual ebb and flow that defines nourishing relationships, is a function of the ventral vagus. As a result of its myelinated pathways, the ventral vagus provides rapid and organized responses. In a ventral vagal state, we have access to a range of responses including calm, happy, meditative, engaged, attentive, active, interested, excited, passionate, alert, ready, relaxed, savoring, and joyful.

This biological need for co-regulation with others is not dissimilar to the concept of limbic revision — “the power to remodel the emotional parts of the people we love,” and to have our own emotional pathways remodeled by the people who love us. This is only possible in safe relationships, and it is the vagus system that governs our sense of safety.

Central to polyvagal theory is the distinction between conscious perception and what Porges termed neuroception — the conditioned way the autonomic nervous system responds from within the body, without our awareness, to cues of safety and danger in the outside world. Because our vagal pathways are shaped by our earliest experiences of co-regulation in the infant-parent dyad, ruptures in that co-regulation — whether by abuse or neglect — condition the dorsal vagus to become dominant and make a neuroception of danger the default response, storying reality away from safety, nowhere more perilously than in intimate relationships. Dana writes:

Co-regulation is at the heart of positive relationships… If we miss opportunities to co-regulate in childhood, we feel that loss in our adult relationships. Trauma, either in experiences of commission (acts of harm) or omission (absence of care), makes co-regulation dangerous and interrupts the development of our co-regulatory skills. Out of necessity, the autonomic nervous system is shaped to independently regulate. Clients will often say that they needed connection but there was no one in their life who was safe, so after a while they stopped looking. Through a polyvagal perspective, we know that although they stopped explicitly looking and found ways to navigate on their own, their autonomic nervous system never stopped needing, and longing for, co-regulation.

Because we are physiologies first and psychologies second, but we are also storytelling and sensemaking creatures, our minds naturally create emotional narratives out of these unconscious vagal states — stories that, if we are not careful enough and conscious enough, may come to subsume reality. Dana observes:

The mind narrates what the nervous system knows. Story follows state.

Our early adaptive survival responses of trauma train the autonomic nervous system on a default neuroception of danger, replacing patterns of connection with patterns of protection in a fear-based narrative. And yet these reflexes can be recalibrated by retraining our regulatory pathways.

Because the feeling of reciprocity is one of the most powerful regulators of the autonomic nervous system, a great deal of repair and rewiring can happen in relationships winged with true reciprocity. Dana writes:

Reciprocity is a connection between people that is created in the back-and-forth communication between two autonomic nervous systems. It is the experience of heartfelt listening and responding. We are nourished in experiences of reciprocity, feeling the ebb and flow, giving and receiving, attunement, and resonance.

But the great paradox is that if our earliest template of connection is marked by rupture and deficient co-regulation, our very notion of reciprocity may be warped, leading us to tolerate immense asymmetries of affection and attention, to mistake deeply imbalanced relationships for reciprocal. The grounds for optimism lie in the very real possibility of changing the template through safe and nourishing relationships — ones we may not so much choose at first, for trauma can taint our choices with unhealthy patterns, as chance into and only then choose to nurture. The payoff is a gradual transition from the dorsal vagal state into the ventral vagal, a gradual willingness to release the patterns of protection in favor of connection, allowing the kinds of relationships Adrienne Rich celebrated as ones “in which two people have the right to use the word ‘love.'”

Complement with the science of how emotion are made and how love rewires the brain, then revisit Toni Morrison on reclaiming the body as an instrument of joy, sanity, and self-love.
